record.paper_title: A survey of open questions in adaptive therapy: bridging mathematics and clinical translation
record.context_brief: Using models to design wet-lab tests
record.original_question: How can mathematical modeling support wet-lab testing of adaptive cancer therapy so that experiments validate theory, assess safety, and guide protocol design for patients? In particular, how should experiments be designed to measure competitive suppression in a cancer; how should drug resistance be represented by mixing pre-evolved resistant and sensitive cells, allowing resistance to evolve during the experiment, using clone tracking, or another approach; and how should treatment algorithms from mathematical or experimental models be translated to clinical practice despite pharmacokinetics, differing animal and patient time scales, toxicity, machine failures, weekends or holidays, and other deviations from planned schedules?

evidence.quote: 2.3 How can we leverage mathematical modelling to support testing of adaptive therapy in the wet lab?
To do so requires experimental platforms for testing and, if necessary, improving the safety and efficacy of adaptive protocols.
Surveying the experimental literature on adaptive therapy, and based on our own experience, we identify three areas in need of further research.
First, how do we design experiments to assess the competitive suppression in a particular cancer and thus the scope for such patients to benefit from adaptive therapy?
Second, there is the question of how drug-resistance is modeled in the wet lab.
Finally, there is the question of how to translate treatment algorithms from mathematical or experimental models into clinical practice.
This raises the question of how robust are adaptive schedules to deviations, and what is the best strategy with which to respond when deviations occur.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Develop a mathematical-modeling framework to support wet-lab testing of adaptive cancer therapy (treatment strategies that exploit competition between drug-sensitive and drug-resistant cancer cell populations by modulating dose to maintain a controlled tumor burden rather than maximizing cell kill). Specifically, address the following three interconnected problems:

(a) Competitive suppression assays. Propose and analyze experimental designs (e.g., co-culture or in vivo mixed-population experiments) together with mathematical models that allow one to quantify the degree to which drug-sensitive cells competitively suppress drug-resistant cells in a given cancer. The design should produce identifiable model parameters (e.g., competition coefficients in a Lotka–Volterra-type system dS/dt = r_S S(1 − (S + α_{SR}R)/K), dR/dt = r_R R(1 − (R + α_{RS}S)/K) − δ(t)·(·), where δ(t) encodes drug effect) that predict whether adaptive scheduling can prolong tumor control compared with continuous maximum-tolerated-dose therapy.

(b) Representation of resistance. Determine, from a modeling and experimental-design standpoint, which representation of drug resistance is most informative and predictive: (i) seeding fixed proportions of pre-evolved resistant cells with sensitive cells, (ii) allowing resistance to evolve de novo during the experiment under selective pressure, (iii) using clone-tracking technologies (e.g., DNA barcoding or lineage tracing) to follow subclonal dynamics, or (iv) an alternative formulation. Provide criteria (identifiability, predictive accuracy on held-out treatment schedules, biological realism) for choosing among these.

(c) Translation to clinical protocols. Given a treatment algorithm derived from in vitro or in vivo mathematical models, formulate a principled procedure for converting it into a clinically deployable protocol that accounts for: pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic differences between model systems and patients; differing intrinsic time scales between animal models and human disease; dose-limiting toxicity; and real-world deviations from planned schedules such as missed doses due to equipment failure, weekends, or holidays. The procedure should include robustness guarantees (e.g., performance bounds under stochastic schedule perturbations) on the resulting clinical protocol.
artifact.status_search_result: This is a broad open research direction posed in a survey on adaptive cancer therapy. While individual components (Lotka–Volterra competition models, barcoded clone-tracking experiments, PK/PD bridging) have been studied, no comprehensive, validated framework integrating experimental design for competitive suppression, optimal resistance representation, and robust clinical translation under schedule perturbations currently exists. The question remains open as a programmatic research agenda.

status_evidence.title: A survey of open questions in adaptive therapy
status_evidence.snippet: Survey identifies leveraging mathematical modelling to support wet-lab testing of adaptive therapy as an open question, with three sub-areas in need of further research.
status_evidence.claim: The problem is explicitly posed as an unresolved research direction in a recent survey.
